title: The pardon-lobbying market and post-pardon SEC dismissals
summary: A paid clemency-lobbying market is well documented. The WSJ (Dec 2025) reported a $1M going rate and success-fee offers of up to $5-6M. NOTUS counted more than $2.1M in 2025 lobbying disclosures that name pardons. NBC reported Fred Daibes paid Keith Schiller's firm $1M, and 60 Minutes filmed Burkman and Wohl pitching a $300K pardon. The SEC dropped its civil cases against Milton, Watson, Ozy and Archer after clemency, and Liz Oyer was fired and replaced by Ed Martin. Several details in the brief need correcting: Watson is not a documented donor, the House Democrats' estimate is now about $1.7B, Stone's $600K from Ver was disclosed as exit-tax lobbying, and Martin left the post in Aug 2026. No grant has been shown to be bought, and the White House denies any pay-to-play.

sub_claims.statement: A paid pardon-lobbying industry has grown around Trump's second term.
sub_claims.finding: NOTUS: federal lobbyists disclosed more than $2.1M in 2025 from clients seeking a 'pardon' or 'clemency', likely an undercount because many pardon lawyers do not register. NBC (Jun 2025) and NPR/NOTUS (Jul 19, 2026) describe a growing business that runs on access to White House aides rather than the DOJ Pardon Office. Paying for advocacy is legal.

sub_claims.statement: Asking prices of $1M or more were reported.
sub_claims.finding: Bloomberg Law (May 2025) found lawyers quoting $1M fees. The WSJ (about Dec 23, 2025; read secondhand) reported $1M as the lobbyists' standard rate, with success fees of up to $6M offered, and said Binance offered up to $5M. NBC: Fred Daibes, convicted of bribing Sen. Bob Menendez, paid $1M to Keith Schiller's Javelin Advisors for 'executive relief' (Q1 2025). He got no pardon and dropped the firm in Jun 2025. The House Judiciary Democrats' Aug 2026 report says intermediaries charged up to $2M per engagement. These are reported fees, not audited prices, and many came from anonymous sources.

sub_claims.statement: Roger Stone, Ches McDowell/Checkmate and Teresa Goody Guillén charged large fees to seek clemency.
sub_claims.finding: McDowell/Checkmate ($450K) and Goody Guillén (about $290K) for Binance's CZ pardon are confirmed (see C36). Stone's $600K from Roger Ver was disclosed as lobbying on the exit tax, so NOTUS left it out of its pardon total. Ver dropped Stone in Dec 2025, and Stone denies lobbying the executive branch on the case. No other named Checkmate pardon client was confirmed. Other documented players: Jack Burkman and Jacob Wohl, paid just under $1M by Joseph Schwartz (Washington Post, via the Daily Beast) and $600K by Boosie BadAzz, who has filed for arbitration to recover $300K; and Keith Schiller (Daibes).

sub_claims.statement: Trump pardoned donors or their relatives: Paul Walczak, Trevor Milton and Changpeng Zhao.
sub_claims.finding: Milton and his wife gave more than $1.8M in Oct 2024, and he was pardoned Mar 28, 2025. Walczak was pardoned Apr 23, 2025, weeks after his mother Elizabeth Fago attended a $1M-per-head Mar-a-Lago dinner (NYT, May 2025). His application cited her fundraising, and the pardon voided about $4.4M in restitution; whether she paid the $1M is unclear. Zhao was pardoned Oct 2025. He is not a documented personal donor: the link runs through Binance's lobbying and its business ties to WLF (see C09).

sub_claims.statement: Carlos Watson's commutation belongs among donor-linked grants.
sub_claims.finding: Trump commuted Watson's roughly 116-month sentence on Mar 28, 2025, hours before he was due to report, which voided about $36M in restitution and about $60M in forfeiture. Watson credited pardon czar Alice Marie Johnson and advocate Glenn Martin. No donation by Watson was found, and the White House gave no justification.

sub_claims.statement: The SEC dropped civil cases after criminal pardons.
sub_claims.finding: The SEC dismissed its civil cases against Milton (Sep 2025), Carlos Watson and Ozy Media (filed about Sep 18-19, 2025) and Devon Archer after clemency, though a pardon does not legally erase civil liability. It later waived penalties for ex-Ozy executives Samir Rao and Suzee Han, citing cooperation. Bloomberg Law (Apr 9, 2026) counts $176M in restitution and fines that pardoned securities-fraud defendants were originally due to pay. The SEC declined comment. A spokesperson quoted by Bloomberg Law said the SEC itself initiated contact to dismiss the Milton case; that article was paywalled and read only through excerpts.

sub_claims.statement: Pardon attorney Liz Oyer was fired, and Ed Martin became pardon attorney.
sub_claims.finding: Then-Deputy AG Todd Blanche fired Oyer on Mar 7, 2025, the morning after she declined to recommend restoring Mel Gibson's gun rights. Then-AG Pam Bondi restored those rights in Apr 2025. Oyer sued on Sep 3, 2026 for reinstatement. Blanche, now Attorney General, says he knew nothing of the Gibson matter. Trump named Ed Martin pardon attorney on May 8, 2025, after Martin's DC US Attorney nomination collapsed. Martin posted 'No MAGA left behind' after the Scott Jenkins pardon. He lost the Weaponization Working Group in Feb 2026, and Trump announced on Aug 21, 2026 that he was leaving to fight election 'Legal Battles'. No successor was found.

sub_claims.statement: House Judiciary Democrats estimate total restitution wiped out at about $1.3B or more.
sub_claims.finding: A Jun 17, 2025 staff memo under Ranking Member Raskin put fines and restitution erased at about $1.3B, roughly $680M of it tied to Milton, whose restitution had not been set. Its caveats: some sums may already have been paid, and collectability is unknown. The Aug 21, 2026 'Pardons, Inc.' report raised the figure to about $1.7B, now including forfeitures. Both are partisan estimates. The White House (Harrison Fields) dismissed the 2025 memo.

sub_claims.statement: Official justifications given for the grants and the process.
sub_claims.finding: The White House says the president acts on his constitutional authority after vetting by the White House Counsel and the DOJ. Leavitt says Trump 'finds it detestable that anyone would even attempt to profit off pardons'. The line 'anyone spending money to lobby for pardons is foolishly wasting their money' is attributed to a spokesperson, variously Lauren Bis or Leavitt. For Schwartz, the White House cited his $5M restitution paid, his poor health and a harsh sentence. For Milton, Trump said he was targeted for supporting him. No justification was given for Watson or Walczak.

sub_claims.statement: Implied: pardons were bought with fees or donations.
sub_claims.finding: Money flows to lobbyists and donations ahead of grants are documented, but no evidence shows Trump granted clemency in exchange for payment. Several big spenders (Daibes, Boosie, Ver on clemency) got nothing. Democrats Rep. Dave Min and Sen. Peter Welch opened a probe on May 7, 2026 with letters to 17 recipients, including David Gentile (commuted; about $15.5M restitution), and escalated on Jun 15, 2026. They lack subpoena power.

corrections: The brief lists Carlos Watson among donor-linked grants; no Watson donation was found. His case ran through Alice Marie Johnson and reform advocates.
The House Judiciary Democrats' $1.3B figure (Jun 2025) was raised to about $1.7B in their Aug 21, 2026 'Pardons, Inc.' report, which also counts forfeitures.
Roger Stone's $600K from Roger Ver was disclosed as exit-tax lobbying, not a pardon, and Ver received a DOJ deferred prosecution deal, not clemency (C36).
Ed Martin is no longer pardon attorney: Trump announced his departure on Aug 21, 2026.
Changpeng Zhao is not a documented personal donor; his link is the Binance lobbying fees and the WLF/USD1 business ties (C09).
Todd Blanche, who fired Oyer as Deputy AG, is now Attorney General; Pam Bondi is described as the former AG.
denials_and_context: White House: clemency is vetted by the White House Counsel and the DOJ and decided by the president. It calls profiting off pardons 'detestable' and says lobbying money is 'foolishly' wasted.
Trump rejected nearly 6,000 clemency applications (Reason, Jul 26, 2026), which argues against a simple pay-for-pardon market.
Paid pardon advocacy is legal and has long existed; the new elements are the scale, the fees and the bypassing of the DOJ Pardon Office.
Many large payments bought no clemency (Daibes $1M, Boosie $600K), and Boosie says he was scammed.
Burkman and Wohl deny wrongdoing. Stone denies lobbying the executive branch on Ver's case. Blanche denies the Gibson link to Oyer's firing.
The restitution totals are partisan estimates with acknowledged caveats (some sums already paid, unclear collectability), and Milton's restitution was never set.
The SEC gave no public rationale for the post-pardon dismissals; critics such as Richard Painter call them political.
